caption_en: 19. Room (6), N wall with wing door (7). Remains of decoration of the fourth style after 62 A.D. Above a faux marble cladding plinth, the middle area is preserved with strong gaps: the yellow central field is framed by a canopy and two green pilasters in a calm architectural view. On the left is a red side field, to which the goal corresponded to on the right. The upper area, above the stucco cornice, has not been preserved. The subject of the central painting is the abandonment of Ariadne by Theseus, to whom she was the

20. Wing (7), N wall (length 4.85 m): same wall as in fig. 20 in its current state of preservation. Although the chromatic layer has been lost, the original subdivision of the wall can be deduced from the still visible traces of the colored lines imprinted in the damp plaster by means of marble rollers.

21. Wing (7), wall N. Reconstructive hypothesis by A. Sikkard, prior to 1882. A classic example of second-style painting from the 70s and 60s BC. The wall is divided with architectural structures and seems to suggest a spatial depth, however it does not have perspective opening. On the green plane of a violet podium rests a row of yellow Ionic columns, soINS. 11, 8-10

22. Long side of the stucco sofa capital of the western pilaster between the fauces (23) and the atrium (27) (width 46 cm). Behind a row of acanthus leaves and drooping lanceolate leaves emerge two large volutes, among which the remains of an acanthus calyx are preserved. About 100 BC.

23. Lower side N of the stucco sofa capital as shown in fig. 22. A] above the drooping leaves rises a calyx formed by three acanthus leaves, flanked by two undulating heart-shaped stems. On the axis is a stem similar to a kerykeèon that reaches up to the balteo of the thin fluted pulvinus. About 100 BC.

24. Room (24), N-W corner. Remains of the stucco decoration of the first style with two rows of ashlars above the orthostats and the top. The ashlars repeat a fixed chromatic sequence: red, ochre, green. DAIB 78.2.094 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

25. Intravertine threshold between the cubicle (24) and the atrium (27) (1.85 x 0.60 m). The thin grooves for fixing the wooden frames of the door are found in all the thresholds installed in the house during the renovations of about 100 BC. Cf. another type of threshold dating back to the rearrangement of 70-60 B.C. in fig. ll.

26. Tetrastyle atrium (27), view from the fauces (23) towards N. Does the lobby cover an area of 124 m? (11.38 x 11.20 m). On the tuff blocks of the edge of the impluvium rest four columns in Nucerino tuff originally stuccoed. Three of them still bear a Corinthian capital. The height of the columns varies between 5.87 and 6.04 m, as, following the excavations, the drums have been rearranged one on top of the other in an arbitrary manner.
28. Atriotetrasstyle (27): capital of S-W, seen from E. Height 68.3 cm. Italic-Corinthian type. About 100 BC.  DAIB 76.3.066 (Fot. P. Grunwald)
27. Atriethrostyle (27): capital of N-E seen from S-E. Height 74.3 cm. Italic-Corinthian type. About 100 BC.  DAIB 83.2.351 (Fot. P. Grunwald)
29. Tetrastyle atrium (27): view from the east wing (32) from the west wing (31). On the right are the tablinum (33) and the entrance hall (34).

30. Tetrastyle atrium (27): view of the N part through the entrance hall (34) on the peristyle (36). On the left, remains of stucco decoration of the first style with fluted corner pilaster of the tablinum (33).

31. Tetrastyle atrium (27), wall E with access to the cubicle (30). Remains of stucco decoration of the first style dating back to about 100 BC, at the bottom large pieces of plaster pertaining to the restoration after 62 AD. DAIB 79.2.070 (Fot. P. Grunwald)
32. Tetrastyle atrium (27), wall E. Remains of the first style decoration (c. 100 BC), which overlap the masonry obstructing the window of the room (30), belonging to an earlier phase.

33. Tetrastyle atrium (27), E. Base of the safe (ark), found empty on 25 October 1834, but in a relatively good state of preservation: "Wooden chest lined with iron and garnished with meanders of various designs executed with bronze nail heads" (Bonnucci 1835, p. 127). Left in situ, the ark has progressively disappeared to the base.
34. Cubicle (28), SE corner: on the left, in wall E, recessed, later walled up, for the head of a bed arranged along the S wall. In the last phase, the room was probably used as a wardrobe.

35. Cubicle (29), wall N. In the last phase (after 62 AD), this room, accessible from both atriums (27) and (3), received a modest decoration of the fourth style. The scheme is currently recognizable only on the N wall: the plinth and the middle area have alternating yellow and red fields, the upper area has a white background. The ornamental motifs are distributed sparingly, the central painting is small (width 38 cm, height 44 cm). See Fig. 36. DAIB 76.3.109 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

36. Cubicle (29), N wall, central painting: unsigned watercolour, in the Museo Naz. of Naples (ADS 379). The couple, often identified as Paris and Oinone, much more likely represents Paris and Helen: the Phrygian shepherd, through the erote, connects to the seated female figure with a hesitant expression and does not move away from it. Later than 62 A.D.

37. Cubicle (29): signino floor; remains of the same type of floor are also found in the adjacent entrance hall (48), which before 70-60 BC formed, together with (29), a larger living room. (c. 100 BC).

38. East Wing (32): signino floor; a meandering edge separates the central carpet from the dotted marginal flounce. The central carpet consists of two strips of diamonds (scutulatum) on the two sides of a rhomboidal field with unknown filling, while in the resulting triangles they are asymmetrical palmettes. (c. 100 BC).

39. Tablinum (33), wall O, extensively restored: the original window overlooking the triclinium (35) was probably walled up after 62 AD. The central pillar is modern. On the sides are the remains of the stucco decoration of the first style. The plinth, restored in the second style, has a curtain motif.

40. Tablinum (33), wall E: same situation as in fig. 39. The mosaic, largely lost and with an emblem that disappeared in the nineteenth century, was made around the years 70-60 BC together with the plinth.

41. Tablinum (33), stucco-decorated field on the E wall: although exposed to the action of the elements since the time of the excavations, the valuable stucco decoration has been preserved to this day. On the right, the edge of the window frame opening onto the entrance hall (34). DAIB 79.2.074 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

42. Exedra (37), view from N. The room, about 5 m deep, opens almost its entire width onto the eastern portico of the peristyle (36). It has a threshold from the period of the first style, a mosaic of the second style and very faded pictorial remains of the fourth style.

43. The peristyle (36), built around the beginning of the first century B.C., is one of the largest in Pompeii. It measures about 23.50 m from W to E, about 27 m from S to N, thus covering an area of 634 m. The roofs of its four porticoes were supported by 8 x 9 columns.  DAIB 79.3.007 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

44. Is the open-air surface of the peristyle (36) 294 m? and was already originally used as a garden (viridarium). Its current layout with a palm tree in the center and a labyrinth of boxwoods has no relation to the original one.

46. Peristyle (36), S. side Example of the most recent type of column with uniform bricks of 3-4 cm in height. These columns are pertinent to the restoration of the peristyle in the years 70-60 B.C. DAIB 79.2.905 (Fot. P. G. FittschenBadura)

45. Peristyle (36), SE corner. All the columns consist of a brick core covered with stucco. Two types of chronologically distinct brick work are used in irregular sequences, testifying to extensive restoration interventions. The oldest type is characterized by layers of varying heights and includes bricks up to 9 cm high.
47. Peristyle (36), N side: the only remains of a Doric stucco capital.
48. Peristyle (36), N portico: the columns have a height of 4.08-4.10 m, with modern concrete abacus and a base diameter of 55 cm; the intercolumns measure 1.63 m cir28

49. Peristyle (36), wall O: the remains of a subdivision of the wall by stucco pilasters with architrave, pertaining to the original decoration of the first style, are preserved, however the finishing layer has large gaps. Traces of

50. Peristyle (36), wall O: detail of the decorative scheme in stucco. The pilasters are placed in correspondence with the columns of the peristyle, but with a width of 51 cm at the base and 43 cm below the capital, 41 cm high, they are more slender. Only the surviving capitals and the architrave are covered with stucco. Almost identical pilasters are found in the second peristyle of the House of the Faun (VI 12, 2; cf. p. 128, fig. 64). Beginning of the first century B.C. DAIB 83.2.360 (Fot. P. Grunwald)
51. Peristyle (36), NE corner: the stucco pilasters on the E wall are in a much worse state than those on the O. DAIB wall 80.2.286 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

52. Peristyle (36), wall E: the pilaster, heavily damaged by atmospheric agents, clearly shows fragments of stucco grooves of columns inside, partly recognizable only by the footprints. This testifies to the reuse of the remains of destroyed columns of the peristyle. c. 70-60 BC.

53. Peristyle (36), N portico: doors to the reception rooms (39), (40), (42) and (43). The brick pillars and side doors of the Corinthian cecus (43) with thresholds of the second type (70-60 BC) can be recognized: evidence of the renovation of the original group of rooms. DAIB 79.2.163 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

54. Triclinium (39): detail of the floor in signino with mosaic threshold between Fanti. room and the hall. The closest comparison is provided by room C of the House of the Griffins in Rome. Both mosaics date back to the first decade of the first century BC.

55. Triclinium (39), wall O, detail: the remarkable wall painting of the second style is partly lost and very faded, however the usual differentiation in the decorative richness between the antechamber and the triclinium proper is evident.

56. Triclinium (39): signino floor and mosaic in the antechamber. The combination of cocciopesto and mosaic of tesserae allows us to attribute this floor to the time of construction of the northern section of the peristyle (36). 100-89 BC

57. Triclinium (39), wall O. Graphic reconstruction of the wall painting (V.M. Strocka - P. Papagialias). See Fig. 55. The forepart plinth and the stucco pilaster protruding from the wall make the triclinium stand out from the sober decoration of the antechamber.

58. Oecus (40), mosaic floor, reconstruction: the vast reception room (4.60 m x 7.60 m) was decorated with a polychrome mosaic, reconstructed by W. Zahn immediately after its discovery on the basis of the parts preserved. A perspective meander surrounds a carpet with axonometric diamonds. The mosaic is contemporary with the rich wall decoration of the second style of 70-60 BC (see fig. 60).
59. Oecus (40), mosaic floor, detail: the N-E angle of the mosaic shown in fig. 58 in its current state of preservation.

60. Oecus (40), wall E, detail: the frescoes, with very faded colors, show an architecturally articulated but closed scheme. On a forepart plinth, in front of yellow orthostats, stand pillars in violet and white-yellow columns surmounted by an epistyle bent at an elbow. The thin violet frieze is decorated, in the area of the capitals, with a chariot race led by Nikai and cupids. The detail clearly shows the connections between the different parts of the fresco, i.e. between the days of work.

61. Cubicle (42), N wall: the decoration is severely deteriorated. However, at the edges of the plaster you can recognize the reduction of the alcove to a length of 2.13 m and the stucco lunette of the vaulted roof.

62. Cubicle (42), mosaic floor. To the W of the Corinthian oecus (43), and accessible from it through a narrow door, is the cubicle (42) located approximately on the central axis of the peristyle (36), on which it opens in almost its entire width. The mosaic with the labyrinth, which gives the house its name (2.06 x 2.06 m) is made of black and white tiles, while the polychrome square emblem (39.5 x 39.2 cm) depicts the fight between Theseus and the Minotaur, which took place in the center of the labyrinth of Knossos. As the wall decoration indicates, the width of the N alcove is smaller than had been foreseen during the previous preparation of the mosaic. 7060 BC

63. Cubicle (42), detail of the emblem of the floor mosaic: in opus vermiculatum (of very small tesserae, measuring just 2 mm on each side), bedded in a travertine box and inserted in the labyrinth mosaic as an independent part. Of the three known replicas of this composition, two are a little older and

64. Cubicle (42), wall O: the best preserved part of the second style wall decoration. On the foreparts of the hoof, there are two tritons on the bow, the one on the left waving an oar, while the other blows into a shell. They support the episttium bent at elbow with a royal with griffins. Between them is a row of veiled columns opening into a view of a courtyard with colonnades. On the opposite side we find a similar representation. '7060 BC
65. Cubicle (42), W wall, plinth: detail of the head of the triton on the left with raised oar.

66. Oecuscorinzio (43), view of part N. This reception room, the largest in the house, is 6.47 m deep and 6.75 m wide. On three sides, at a distance of 66 cm from the walls, there are a total of ten brick columns covered with stucco, none of which has been preserved in their entirety. The low ceiling of the corridor is at a height of 3.50 m. The central part of the room was probably covered by a segmented barrel vault covered with stucco, the key to which is at a height of about 5.35 m from the mosaic.

67. Oecuscorinzio (43), E-wall. The walls still preserve remarkable remains of grandiose compositions of architectural views of the second style. The E and W walls have views of the courtyard of a temple with thòlos, which correspond as reflected images; In front of the tent that hangs in the middle of the visual axis is an altar with a sacrificial wild boar, while on the sides in front of the partition walls are placed precious votive amphorae or accessories for ceremonies or partridges are hung as gifts from guests. The rigidly axial composition of the side walls does not take into account the doors or the diverging columns. A harmony between the arrangement of the columns and the painted view is, however, appreciable from the place of honor of the triclinium, from the imus in medio "consolare".
68. Corinthian Oecus (43), wall E, detail: inside a thòlos consecrated to an unidentified deity hangs a circle lamp with a fluttering bird.

69. Oecuscorinzio (43), wall E: among the sumptuously decorated gilded columns are silver amphorae with relief scenes. On the wall-partition is depicted a mask of Pan. On the right, two partridges are hanging from a rope.

71. Oecuscorinzio (43), N face, third on the right. On the N wall was painted a composition corresponding symmetrically to the arrangement of the columns. Of this, a variant in a better state of preservation is known from cubicle M of the Villa of Fannius Synistor in Boscoreale (currently in New York, Metropolitan Museum): two urban landscapes frame a view of a sacred area.
70. Corinthian Oecus (43), E wall, detail. Preliminary tracing (sinopia) on the preparatory layer of the plaster. This is an early sketch of the composition, not the final drawing.
72. Corinthian oecus (43): emblem in opus sectile (25.5 x 25.5) in the center of the room. The emblem, of the III style, was inserted in the mosaic of the II style in the Tiberian era.

73. Secondary triclinium (44), S. The room, accessible only from the oecus (43), was used as a triclinium of minor importance. The segmented barrel vault key is at a height of 4.45 m above the floor. The walls have a simple decoration of II style fields.

74. Secondary triclinium (44), floor: mosaic emblem. The opus vermiculatum, of high quality, represents the result of a cockfight in the gymnasium, reflected respectively in the joy for the victory and in the sadness of the two young owners of the animals. The mosaic found a secondary location in the room (44) during the renovations of 7060 BC.

75. Cubicle (45), wall E. Measured at the keystone of the stucco lunette, the height of the room is 4.50 m. As soon as the execution of the decorations in the second style was completed, the external wall was attacked by humidity; for this reason it was isolated by means of tegulae mammatae (to which the vertical grooves in the cladding are to be related) and plastered and painted again with an identical composition, of which, however, only the plinth is preserved.

76. Cubiculum (45), S wall, detail: on the green predella of a plinth with ochre, red-brown € violet compartments, a partition wall with orthostats with fake yellow, red and light violet marble cladding is depicted, surmounted by a frieze with dentilled cornices interrupted by pillars with vertical bands supporting an epistyle bent at an elbow. In the empty space above the partition walls, green garlands hang on an ochre background. Above the lintel, the surface of the wall was blue.

77. Cubicle (45), SE corner. Since the left corner pillar of the S wall had been obliterated by the reinforcing wall lining to the E wall, it was carried out again, thus reducing the surface of the wall.

78. Cubicle (45): mosaic emblem in travertine box; Of insignificant size (26.1 x 26.1 cm), but of high quality, this vermiculatum mosaic depicts a dove extracting a jewel from an open basket. The emblem found a secondary place in the room (45) during the renovation of 7060 BC.

79. Cubicle (46), W wall. Located to the E of the Corinthian oecus (43), with which it communicates through a door, this room is a pendant to (42) and opens for almost its entire width onto the E portico of the peristyle (36).
80. Cubicle (46), W wall (with alcove). Free watercolour reconstruction by L. Gruner, before 1850 (London, Victoria & Albert Museum, Box A 40, Fol. 17852).
81. Cubicle (46), wall O, detail: a pair of birds is depicted on the curtain behind the partition wall. Worthy of note is the erroneous perspective rendering of the colonnade that closes the view.

82. Cubicle (46), wall E. Following the experience with the E wall of the room (45), this external wall was isolated from the beginning with tegulae mammatae, as evidenced by the remains of the adjacent frescoes. The decoration had to correspond to that of the O wall.
83. Cubicle (46), N wall, part O: decorative band above the orthostats.

84. Cubicle Alcove (46). In contrast to the cubicle (42), the large alcove (2.28 x 1.53 m) is located here on the median axis of the room. The remains of the lunette allow us to establish that the key of the segmented vault was at a height of 3.60 m.

85. Cubicle alcove (46), reconstructive drawing (V.M. Strocka - P. Papagialias). The plinth consists of a row of arches, through which a lively aquatic landscape could be glimpsed. Ionic columns stand in front of closed walls of fake polychrome marble; in the space between the orthostats and the mouldings is a singular frieze composed of thirty-three figured ashlars. It depicts twelve ithyphallic fàtaikoi, apotropaic spirits and protectors of fertility, eleven erotes belonging to Venus, and ten busts, among which a satyr, three Horai (?) and a veiled matron (Juno?) can be recognized, while the remaining five, perhaps Venus, the Charites and Bacchus, are preserved in an incomplete state.
86. Cubicle (46), alcove: detail of the right half of the O. Wall Ash of the frieze with erotes between two female figures (Horai?) and two pàtaihoi.
88. Cubicle (46): "bedside" mosaic of the alcove, with black and white tiles. (70-60 BC).
87. Cubicle (46): floor mosaic with black and white tiles. (70-60 BC).

89. View through the courtyard (10), in a northerly direction, of the stable (11), the exedra (12) walled up in 62 AD, the cubicle (14) and the corridor (15), leading to the kitchen, the bakery and the administrator's house.
90. Kitchen (13): hearth and lararium niche in the S-E corner.

91. Kitchen(13): view of part O, with door to the room (12), sink (fusorium), fountain, drainage channel of the three basins for hot water (miliaria) originally located above the praefurnium of the bathroom. In their place today is the erroneous reconstruction of a second hearth.
92. Cubicle (14), N wall: remains of a decoration of the first style. Probably the cook's bedroom.

93. Apodyterium - frigidarium (20), wall N. The warehouse that originally opened onto the courtyard (16) was annexed to the bathroom, when it was enlarged and again decorated in the third style; on this occasion the N wall was closed. When its use as a bathroom ceased, as a result of the earthquake of 62 AD, the room (20) became a bakery warehouse with a new passage to the courtyard (16). DAIB 76.3.082 (Fot. P. Grunwald) 94. Apodyterium - frigidarium (20), wall E: on the right is the entrance to the antechamber (59), with decorations of the third style, on the left the later opening onto the courtyard (16).
94. Apodyterium - frigidarium (20), wall E: on the right is the entrance to the antechamber (59), with decorations of the III style, on the left the later opening onto the courtyard (16).

95. Apodyterium - frigidarium (20): watercolour of the III style decoration by F. Boulanger (1837-38; Paris, École Nationale Supérieure des Beaux Arts). The wall paintings of 20-30 AD are now in a very poor state of preservation. The French architect Boulanger immortalized them when their condition was still good, however he reproduced the middle area from the W wall and the upper area from the E. Hanoune - de Vos 1985, Tav. IV, 2

96. Tepidarium (21), E wall. The stucco in relief of the lunette, which shows the trophies for the athletes, is preserved in good condition, while the stucco covering of the ceiling, with its delicate articulation, and the wall paintings are largely incomplete. On the left you can see the remains of the concameration system.

97. Tepidarium (21): detail of the surviving marginal area of the stucco cladding of the vault on the E. Ovoli cornices of particular finesse delimit fields of different sizes arranged at right angles.

98. Tepidarium (21), wall E: watercolour by Danish architect Martin Nyropp (18491921). Certainly a hundred years ago the state of preservation of the wall was much better than the current one, however the return of the plinth is not adherent to the original, but the result of a free reconstruction (KoPenagca Kunstakademie, A 324).
99. Tepidarium (21), left half of wall O: watercolour by the Swedish architect Frederick Wilhelm Scholander (1816-1881), made in 1843, cf. fig. 98 (Stockholm, Nationalmuseum 1399, 1882).
101. Caldarium (22), view of the S-E part. On the left, niche E; on the right, the niche S enlarged during the redecoration of the room in the III style.

100. Caldarium (22), apse of the W wall: on a black plinth with two hawks among green bushes is a fence, above which there is a garden landscape with birds and two lying sphinxes. III style (20-30 AD).
102. Caldarium(22):upper area of decoration in the III style in the niche E. Fot. Fr. Grunwald

103. Caldarium (22), detail of the N wall of niche E: pilaster decoration of the III style. Watercolour by Danish architect L.A. Winstrup (1849) (Kopenhagen, Kunstakademie, A 6107). Photos. Kunstakademisches Museum Copenhagen

104. Courtyard (16), converted into a bakery after 62 AD View of the N part: three millstones are partially preserved; The presence of a fourth, which has been lost, can be deduced from the gap in the basalt pavement, in the foreground on the right.

105. Bakery (16), view of the S part: on the left, the W wall of the peristyle (36) and the corridor (15); on the right, the staircase (59) leading to the upper floor above the bathroom and access to the room (20) in the last phase.

106. Bakery (16), E-wall. Next to the passage between the reception rooms (39)-(16) and the bathroom (20)-(22), walled up during the preparation of the oven, there is a podium. Contrary to what is usually claimed, it is not a hearth; As indicated by the remains of a lead pipe protruding from its upper part and the shallow basins located on the right, it was used to supply the water supply of the oven. This interpretation is supported by the presence of the river god Sarno in the painting, which is very deteriorated, which also depicts the Pompeian Venus with Cupid and Vesta with the donkey between two Lares.

107. Administrator's House VI 11, 8, Environment (56), Part O. On the left, in the foreground, the access to the courtyard (16), and then to the manor house; on the right, the staircase to the upper floor; behind the wall, below the staircase, the latrine; on the opposite side, probably, a hearth.

108. Administrator's House VI 11, 8, atrium (50), wall N. Remains of the oldest masonry of the entire complex. Made of limestone opus incertum between Sarno limestone piers, probably at the beginning of the second century BC, but already repaired in ancient times. The painting with the Lares in the niche has been lost for a long time. DAIB 83.2.372 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

109. Administrator's House VI 11, 8, atrium (50), part E. The floor preserves 1 remains of an impluvium in signino. In the background, on the left, the triclinium (54), on the right the apotheca (?) (53). DAIB 83.2.373 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

110. Administrator's house VI 11.8, living room (52), wall O with window placed at the top and simple painting in areas completely deteriorated. Ceiling height from the floor: 2.50 m. The holes on the right are certainly to be placed in relation to looting after 79 A.D. (see fig. 73).

111. Travertine weight with iron handle, 16.5 kg = 50 pounds Roman. Height 15 cm, major diameter 26.2 cm. Found in the stairwell that leads from the room (2) to the cellar. The engraved inscription bearing the name of its owner P(ublius) SEX(tilius) also reveals the name of the last owner of the House of the Labyrinth. DAIB 80.2.430 (Fot. P. Grunwald) V.M. St.

1. Tablinum (5), S wall: on a layer of white plaster, pertaining to the decoration of the first style, to which that of the pillar visible on the left is also referable, a decoration of the third style was laid with a plinth and red middle area articulated in panels; The gaps in the white upper area allow the previous layer to be seen tapped to make the later plaster adhere. A yellow floor and a molded stucco frame complete the decoration.

2. Triclinium (6): on the N wall only the lower part at the plinth and part of the middle area was redecorated with red square panels, which preserved two rows of ashlars, the shelves and the moulded stucco frame from the first style decoration.
3. Triclinium (6): in the E section of the S wall are also visible the edges of the stapled carpet of the redecoration in the fourth style, with red squared panels. 80 N61073

4. Triclinium (6): the W wall preserved the first style decoration in its entirety, until the last period of the house's life, with a yellow plinth, a middle area with orthostats surmounted by two rows of ashlars and a top above.

5. Cubicle (16): the fall of the plaster from wall E highlighted the solid wall structure in opus square of limestone blocks, covered with a decoration of the first style with a yellow plinth and a red top; part of the molded stucco cornice that crowned the middle area remains.

6. Cubicle (16): the S wall retains, above the yellow plinth, part of the middle area with a single long orthostat with a stucco relief garland, surmounted by a row of ashlars and the complex stucco moulded frame with an internal structure of tiles.
7. Wing (18), wall E: in section S there is a painting with an architectural landscape. 80 61080
8. Wing (18), wall E: of the decoration of the IV style on a white background, part of the red medallion remains in section N. 80 N61081

1. Oecus(5), N wall: green plinth; the yellow middle area had a central aedicule with a painting, of which it is only possible to recognize the width (0.60 m), flanked by narrow red compartments. 80 N61079
2. Oecus(6), N wall: illegible plinth; red middle area with a perspective winged aedicule with candelabra, separated from the yellow side panels by compartments closed at the bottom by partitions.
3. Triclinium (7): cocciopesto floor with dotted with large white tesserae.

4. Triclinium (7), S wall: the black plinth has geometric elements in the central panel of the plants and in the side panels; in the red middle area, the central aedicule is separated from the side panels by narrow compartments; the color of the upper area is no longer distinguishable.

5. Triclinium (7), wall O: the black plinth is divided into panels, the central one with plants, and the sides with a single-line carpet border and animals, separated by narrow compartments; the middle area has an aedicule with a yellow background in the center and red panels crossed by thin candelabra on the sides.
6. Triclinium (7), W wall, S section: detail of the black plinth with griffin facing right.
7. Cubicle (9), N wall with splayed window open to the atrium: black plinth; white middle area with yellow and red square panels; white upper area with red squares. 80 N61089

1. Main façade of the House of the Faun on the Via della Fortuna, from E. Like many major and minor residences in Pompeii, this one also has a row of shops on the main façade; Located on one of the most important and busiest roads, these enjoyed an advantageous position that the owner knew how to exploit economically. However, as far as we know, it is in the House of the Faun that the main exterior is architecturally configured as a pillar façade for the first time. Built in the first half of the second century.

2. The main entrance, at no. 2 of the house, had a particular prominence in the context of the pillared façade. Corner pillars with carefully worked capitals of the Corinthian order, instead of the simple and usual Tuscan, support an autonomous entablature and frame a shallow vestibule, open to the street. The masonry work pertaining to this intervention is clearly distinguished from the old tuff pillars. Here too there are few remains of stucco on pilasters, walls and even on the worn tuff pillars.

5. Front W on Vico del Fauno, from S. The side facades of the House of the Faun were closed. On closer inspection, only high slits reflected the internal subdivision. The opus incertum masonry was characterized by high plinths covered with fine white plaster, which was renewed several times, but not pertinent to the first construction phase of the house.

7. Façade E on the Vico del Labirinto: also on façade E [in the context of the room (25)] a trace of the original pillar decoration is preserved. Evidently it existed only above the projecting plinth.

6. N façade on Vico di Mercurio, N-E corner: the masonry of the N-E corner testifies to the later transformations undergone by the house, following which the rooms to the N of the second peristyle (39) received an upper floor. During the same works, the rear exit was also opened, at number 7. To the west of this remains part of a plastered pillar, demonstrating that once even the side facades had an architectural subdivision.

8. Workshop (4), with entrance from no. 6: the masonry of the easternmost workshop (4) on the Via della Fortuna documents a particularly eventful construction history. In the original construction of the second century BC, and in all subsequent phases, the workshop was equipped with a fergula, illuminated by a slit window in the E wall. The numerous beam holes in the E-wall belong to this first construction phase. In the S-E corner there are small remains of the first style wall decoration in green.

9a-c. Fauces (53), of the entrance to number 2: compared to the vestibule (26), decorated in a very simple form of the first style, the fauces (53) were sumptuously decorated. The large door that opened to the outside was framed, like the passage to the atrium, by elegant panels and pillars in imitation marble, while the side walls were accentuated by a valuable decoration in the first style, of which large passages are preserved (see fig. 84d). The plinth, which equalizes the difference in floor level, was renovated in the third style. Here, we probably find the continuation of the decoration partially preserved on both sides of the door, consisting of a wine-red plinth, a narrow intermediate band, a diamond motif and a meandering marginal band. In the middle area, on the side walls there are high orthostats, two head and one cut, with double relief edges. The surfaces of the orthostats are imitation of alabaster-type marble, while the double edge is in solid color. This detail, together with the characteristics of the marble imitation, emphasizes the absence of references to real models, and the clear pre-eminence of the decorative value itself. A double "perspective" Doric kyma is surmounted by a further row of low head and cut ashlars, also in imitation marble and with a double edge. Above the projecting architrave with frame is a frieze, currently smooth, to which metal supports were attached in the past (perhaps in the shape of lions or sphinxes?); these supported dentilled corbels, in turn supporting a coffered cornice, the support surface of a miniature temple façade rendered in three dimensions, consisting of the four-column vestibule of a Corinthian prostyle temple. However, most of the columns and pediments have been lost. The walls of the cella of the temple, divided by smooth pilasters, were decorated in the first style.

15. Main atrium (27), overview from S. From the fauces you can enjoy the view of the main atrium with impluvium in the center, in which is housed a copy of the statuette of the Dancing Faun preserved in the Naz. of Naples. 17. Main atrium (27), E wall and E wing (30). Although it was largely destroyed, the first-style decoration on the narrow piers between the entrance doors from the atrium to the cubiculum (see Fig. 84a, no. 27) can be reconstructed in detail from old photographs. The plinth, which perhaps originally had a decoration of waving ribbons, was renewed with rough marble imitations probably of the III style. Above the plinth, bordered by a thin band, follow horizontal orthostats framed by strips, another thin band and a row of ashlars framed by a molded frame. The rows of low ashlars arranged at the head and cut, which continue up to the probable cornices crowning the wall, were interrupted by a cornice at the height of the lintel of the door. Of the frames, however, only the holes for fixing them remain. As for the colors, next to black and white, evidence of the presence of wine red, green and yellow is still recognizable or handed down. Only the black orthostats were perhaps marbled. Underneath some parts of the wall decoration, thin sheets of lead had been applied with numerous iron nails and directly on the masonry, whose function was probably to prevent the appearance of cracks on the large surfaces of smooth stucco. Judging by the proportions of the tablinum pillars, the considerable height of the walls of the atrium was probably divided into two registers, the upper of which, above the ashlar decoration of the first style, bore an order of Ionic semi-columns (a similar example in the atrium of the Samnite House of Herculaneum). 21. Third cubiculum (32), on the W side of the main atrium (27): in this cubiculum the decoration in the first style has been preserved in an unusually good state (see fig. 84a, no. 32). In the sequence of plinth, band, horizontal orthostats and row of ashlars, the usual band above the orthostats is missing, which, like the ashlars above, are molded and separated from each other by incisions. The color gamut is similar to that of the atrium. This is followed by a projecting architrave with molding at the upper edge, a frieze area that has lost the surface layer, and a dentilled cornice. Above this are two narrow slits with plaster remains, once probably framed by molded stucco cornices. There is a lack of reference points for a reconstruction of the upper register of the walls. It seems that numerous restorations, especially in the plinth, took place in the period following the earthquake of 62 AD.

The threshold divided into three parts by the dadiform pedestals of the exedra distila of the Mosaic of Alexander, is bordered by a purple frame of at least five rows of tesserae on the side of the exedra. We see plants and ducks reflected in a body of water flowing along the barely hinted shore with a few tufts of vegetation near the viewer. These are two porphyriones (top right) and four ducks, one of which launches itself towards a frog sitting on a lotus leaf (Nelumbo nucifera). The plant with floating leaves protruding from the water is depicted with great precision, in the different phases of its cycle: bud, flower, infructescence with the capsule containing the edible seeds. The kingfisher (bottom right) perched near the shore, on a similar infructescence, is not intent on fishing but is peering at the steep bank where it uses to dig its nest. The second duck from the left is replicated as it is with reflection in the water below, in the threshold of the central intercolumnium (see the following figure). Diap. MNN s.n.

54. Exedra (37), floor, threshold: section at the central intercolumnium: vermiculatum emblem (now in the Museo Naz. in Naples, inv. 9990b; 66x333 cm) depicting a Nilotic landscape with six swimming ducks forming the background to three pairs of animals facing each other on the bank: ichneumon and cobra, hippopotamus and crocodile, and two ibises. The shelduck (Tadorna tadorna) with its head made of blue glass (?) tiles, depicted behind the cobra is repeated in the restoration patch on the right of the stroke, made by an inexperienced hand. The outline of the shore under the hippopotamus is formed by a row of black tesserae, characteristic of the mosaic workshop at work in the house. Grasses (alpha and Phragmites australis) sprout from the sandy shore. The animals cast shadows to the right, in correspondence with the natural light of the environment, which entered from the S-W. The two ibises on the right belong to the species Threskiornis aethiopicus or sacred ibis. As for crossed beaks, with such skirmishes male specimens tend to solve territorial issues in the mating season; but the depiction does not exclude that here we are dealing with the preliminaries of an approach between male and female.

58. Exedra (37) of the first peristyle, wall E: incorrect restoration work has upset the original relationships between the remains of the wall decoration. At one time, this decoration of the first style also corresponded substantially to the scheme already known and described several times, although made with much greater attention to detail (see fig. 84b, no. 37). The original plinth was replaced by a painted curtain, now lost, similar to the one visible in one of the cubicula (31). Above it were vertical orthostats bordered at the top by a row of head and shear bosses; below the upper cornice (evidenced only by the presence of holes for its fixing) are two other rows of ashlars. The richness of the decoration, corresponding to that of the floor, consisted above all in the many marble imitations of orthostats and ashlars, in the figurative representations (centaurs, birds, vases) and in the valuable framing bands.

59. Exedra (37), wall E, frieze between plinth and middle area, detail: watercolour depicting part of a ashlar painted in faux relief of yellow veined marble, with the drunkenness of the Centaurs during the wedding of Pirithous and Hippodamia. The Centaurs casting shadows on the left were monochromes in cinnabar red on a white background. This rare example of the first figurative style remained in situ, has become illegible for more than a century due to lack of conservation measures. The anonymous watercolor executed immediately after the excavation (1831), shows three crouching Centaurs and one standing pointing their hand towards the battle (lost without being documented) taking place between the Lapiths and their fellow Centaurs who have kidnapped Pirithous' wife and the women of the guests. This moment of the centauromachy, which does not appear in the very rich iconography of this myth, is recalled by Ovid (Met., 12.240241): ardescunt germani caedi bimembres, Icertatim omnes uno ore 'arma, arma' loquuntur), probably in the wake of the passage cited by Athenaeus (Deipn.,, 11.476c) of the lost tragedy Perrhaebides by Aeschylus. The Centaur standing on the right pours wine from the wineskin into his companion's sk)phos, helping himself as described by Pindar (fig. 166) after having swept away the milk served on the table. The jar overturned under the Centaur with the wineskin perhaps alludes to this not secondary episode of the event, given that the passage from milk to wine to which 1 Centaurs were not accustomed, was at the root of the rape of women. The Centaur seen from the front holding a kàntharos in his left hand, has his left leg bent in front of his chest. The companion seen from the back, more attentive to the battle than to the wine that is poured for him, wears a cloak that camouflages the transition between human and animal accentuated by the twisted position. His body is surrounded by a crown of red symposiast's leaves, like the Centaur who pours him a drink. They all wear the pine crown on their temples, more congenial to the habitat of these torrential beings of the mountains. An exhibition with precious metal vessels (situlae, kjathos, oinochòe, phiàle) located behind a crater adorned with leaves sprouting from the foot, closes the scene on the right, confirming the importance given to wine. ADS 405 (Fot. Pedicini) M. d. V.

60. Corridor (38) between the first and second peristyle: the secondary rooms of the House of the Faun were also embellished with valuable floors and wall decorations of the first style. One of the few surviving examples is found in the corridor (38) between the first and second peristyles. Compared to the "exedra of Alexander", this decoration is undoubtedly much simpler and therefore documents a hierarchy in investments in the decoration of the house, proportional to the importance of the individual rooms (see fig. 84c, no. 38). A smooth plinth (without plinth) is bordered at the top by a narrow band; in the middle area, the wall has a uniform scansion in simple orthostats; The indication of the marginal strips and the joints between them is entrusted only to engraved lines. This decoration is concluded by the frame of a probable moulded relief architrave, now lost. The simplicity is found both in the details of the decoration and in the use of color, which does not aim to obtain faux marble effects and is limited to white only, except for the red band (as far as it is preserved). 75. Small exedra (50) of the second peristyle (40). Given the greater availability of space, increasing in the SW direction, niches and exedras of different depths were carved into the back wall of the N portico of the second peristyle. In the minor exedra, at the height of the third column from the W, there are conspicuous remains of the first style wall decoration (see fig. 84d, no. 50). The exedra was framed by Tuscan pillars, which perhaps originally supported a vaulted roof. The walls were divided into plinths, bands and vertical orthostats, in which blocks arranged at the head alternated, according to the scheme of the fauces. The decoration ended at the top with an architrave. In addition to the usual colors (black, white, wine red and green), we know of the use of marble imitations (partly alabaster) on pillars and orthostats. DAIR 61.3162

76. Large niche for statues (49) of the second peristyle (40). On the occasion of a renovation (around the beginning of the first century A.D.?), a niche for statues was built in the center in the N wing of the second peristyle, which constituted the central point of a symmetrical sequence of niches and exedras. Among other things, an older exit on the Vico di Mercurio was sacrificed to this intervention. However, it seems that the set-up of this new exposed façade was never completed. Only remains of the lower layer of plaster are preserved.

77. Small niche E for statues (47) of the second peristyle (40). This small room was also converted into a niche for statues by adding a coarsely made base. The later transformation into a wardrobe-room, to which the plaster in the upper area of the wall and the grooves for the shelves are to be referred, probably took place only in the last phase of the city's life, after the earthquake of 62 AD. In the lower area there are remains of the original wall decoration in the first style (see fig. 84d, no. 47), demonstrating that initially the secondary rooms of the House of the Faun had also been carefully decorated. The scheme is the usual one: an orthostat plinth with engraved edges and joints, surmounted by a protruding band. Above the plinth were orthostats, a band, other rows of ashlars and final cornices. Worthy of note are the orthostats of the faux marble plinth, made with a different technique from that usually attested in the House of the Faun, that is, with green, yellow and red speckling on a black and red background. 78. Secondary exit at no. 7 and cubiculum (45) of the second peristyle (40). No traces of wall decoration are preserved, not even on the walls to the E of the N portico of the second peristyle, reconstructed on the occasion of the interventions already described, and it is therefore doubtful, or rather improbable, that the previous decorative scheme with pillars could have been restored. On the back walls there is the simple plaster of the rooms on the upper floor, restored in the same period. DAIR 61.3167

80. Kitchen (24) with fireplace block. Above the hearth, in front of the E wall, at the time of the above-mentioned renovations, two new windows were opened at different heights, clearly distinct from the old slit windows. The walls were covered with smooth plaster.

79. Kitchen (24) with lararium. The N wall of the kitchen of the House of the Faun, probably renovated only after the earthquake of 62 AD, has a projecting aedicule-lararium, now unusually located high up due to a further change in floor level. Its careful workmanship is in stark contrast to the smooth and chrome plaster of the wall. Its formal elements (e.g. capitals of Tuscan pillars) and the quality of the workmanship indicate that it belongs to an older phase of cuisine, datable around the end of the first century BC, i.e. to the period of the second late style. In the W section of the room, as shown by the footprints in the structure, a gallery was added, also located very high.

82. Latrine (20). The S-shaped latrine of the bathroom also dates from the last construction phase of the house. Here, as in the adjacent rooms, the masonry bears witness to several previous construction periods. Only remains of the first style wall decoration are preserved. In the last phase, the coating consisted of a simple plaster.

81. Bathroom (22) with hypocaust remains. The bathroom, equipped with a hypocaust and consisting of two rooms to the S of the kitchen, replaced an older bathroom probably only after the earthquake of 62 AD. To allow hot air to enter from the kitchen, the floor level had to be lowered. However, it seems that these works have not been completed, as evidenced, for example, by the total absence of traces of the use of the heating system.

83. Servile sector, from S (17)(19). The many constructive interventions that followed one another in the servile sector of the house, from time to time inspired by technical innovations or dictated by changes in needs, never affected the basic organization of the house. In all periods, a long passage, parallel to the first peristyle, made the servant rooms accessible. An intermediate room (17), often rebuilt with different functions, served as a connection with the secondary atrium (7). The walls were covered with a light plaster with a red plinth, the dating of which is impossible to specify.

53. Triclinium (q), W wall, central section: the painting, now lost, was seen by Maue and was later reproduced by G. Discanno. In the background of a landscape are a man and a woman embracing, on the left is a warrior, on the right a woman holds the crowd, in the middle is a tetrastylon with a staircase that encloses a platform with an altar on which logs burn, a rectangular structure and another round rise in the background. Athena, from above, presides over the scene. The figures involved were variously interpreted; the Mau supposed it was the meeting between Jason and Medea in Colchis; Hermann argued that it was not necessarily the meeting of two lovers (Protesilaus and Laodamia, Jason and Medea, Orestes and Iphigenia); later Dawson proposed the identification with Demophon and Phyllis, Lehmann suggested that it could be the meeting and marriage between Harmony and Cadmus on the island of Samothrace, in front of the sanctuary of Hecate, an event that was annually represented in the rites; the hypothesis of this interpretation is strengthened by the subjects that make the pendant, in particular that of the S wall which represents the meeting between Hero and Leander. "It is possible that the owner commissioned the decorator to compose a decorative program for the exedra... that commemorated his journey of salvation to Samothrace and initiation into the mysteries".
